summary: Explains the idea of a network transport circuit breaker, why tunnels and applications using non-congestion-controlled traffic need them, and what requirements one must meet. It is a BCP.

plainLanguage.summary: A network transport circuit breaker is a safety switch for traffic that does not slow down when a link gets busy. It watches how much traffic enters and how much comes out, and if the difference stays large for long enough, it stops the traffic. It is a last resort, used only when ordinary congestion control has not solved the problem.

subtitle: A last-resort safety switch that cuts off traffic causing persistent, excessive congestion when nothing else slows it down.

tldr.problem: Traffic that does not respond to congestion, such as many UDP applications and traffic inside tunnels, can keep a link overloaded and starve the traffic that does respond.
tldr.mechanism: A circuit breaker meters traffic at an ingress point and an egress point, compares the two over a long measurement period, and when persistent excessive congestion is detected it terminates or sharply reduces the traffic.
tldr.outcome: Other flows on the same path keep working while the unresponsive traffic is cut off. RFC 8084 is an Internet Best Current Practice.

facts.label: Measurement period
facts.value: Longer than the time congestion control needs to reduce its rate

facts.label: Reaction severity
facts.value: A reduction of at least an order of magnitude

facts.label: Example trigger
facts.value: More than 10% loss over three successive measurements

facts.label: SAToP measurement period
facts.value: 1 second, with more than three Severely Errored Seconds

today: RFC 8084 is an Internet Best Current Practice, published in March 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so the guidance stands as written.

sections.title: What a Circuit Breaker Is For
sections.content:
The term comes from electricity supply, and has nothing to do with network circuits. An electrical circuit breaker is a protection mechanism of last resort: under normal circumstances it should not be triggered, and it exists to protect the supply network and attached equipment when there is an overload.

The same principle works in networking, to avoid persistent excessive congestion affecting other flows that share network capacity. Persistent congestion was a feature of the early Internet of the 1980s, where excess traffic starved other connections. It was countered by requiring congestion control in TCP, and that requirement is what kept the Internet stable. TCP was by far the dominant traffic then, but that is no longer the case, and non-congestion-controlled traffic, including many applications using UDP, can now form a significant proportion of the traffic on a link.

A network transport circuit breaker is an automatic mechanism that continuously monitors a flow or an aggregate of flows, detects when they experience persistent excessive congestion, and then terminates the flow or significantly reduces its rate. This is a safety measure that prevents network resources being starved and other flows being denied access. Such measures are essential for a heterogeneous Internet and for traffic that is hard to predict in advance, and they reduce the potential for congestion collapse, as described in RFC 2914.

There are important differences between a transport circuit breaker and a congestion control method. Congestion control, as implemented in TCP, SCTP and DCCP, operates on a timescale of about one packet round-trip time, and it can also detect congestion from Explicit Congestion Notification marks. It reacts by continuously adapting the transmission rate, and it works on individual flows such as a five-tuple. A circuit breaker is recommended for non-congestion-controlled flows and for traffic aggregates such as a tunnel. It operates on timescales much longer than the round-trip time and triggers under abnormal congestion. People have been building what this document calls circuit breakers on an ad hoc basis, so the document provides guidance on deploying them.

The conditions that cause a circuit breaker to trigger ought to be regarded as abnormal. Examples include anomalous traffic that exceeds the provisioned capacity, traffic generated by an application while the provisioned capacity is being used for something else, routing changes that put more traffic on the monitored path, misconfiguration of a service or network device, and a misconfigured admission controller or policer that allows more traffic than expected.

Other mechanisms are available to operators to detect excessive congestion, such as watching the utilisation of a port. They can react over a shorter timescale than a circuit breaker, and the circuit breaker remains the method of last resort, triggered only when those other reactions failed to reduce the congestion.

In many cases the reason for a trigger will not be evident to the source of the traffic, and the circuit breaker cannot signal back to the impacted applications, which may have difficulty learning that it happened and where. Application developers are therefore advised to deploy appropriate congestion control where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic does not slow down when a link gets crowded, and that traffic can push everything else off the link. A circuit breaker is a safety net for that case. It watches a long stretch of time, not a single moment, so it does not cut traffic off for an ordinary busy spell.

sections.title: The Parts of a Circuit Breaker
sections.content:
The basic design involves communication between an ingress point, where traffic is sent, and an egress point, where it is received. A circuit breaker controls traffic passing through a subset of the routers between the two points, and the path between them may be a tunnel or another network-layer technique. One expected use is at the ingress and egress of a service, where all the traffic being considered terminates beyond the egress point, so the ingress and egress carry the same set of flows. The ingress and egress functions may also sit in the endpoints themselves.

The components needed are:

  • An ingress meter at the sender or tunnel ingress, recording the number of packets and bytes sent in each measurement interval. It measures the load the network is being offered. The interval could be many seconds, or a series of shorter measurements combined by the measurement function.
  • An egress meter at the receiver or tunnel egress, recording the number and bytes received in each interval. It measures the load the network is supporting, and it may use other signals as well, such as loss or congestion marking experienced on the path. The measurements at the two ends can be synchronised, with an offset for the time of flight or a reference to a particular packet, so that the counters cover the same span of packets.
  • A method for communicating the measured values from both meters to the measurement function. This could be return measurement packets or control messages from the receiver to the trigger function at the sender, an operations, administration and management mechanism, an in-band signalling datagram, or a pure control-plane function such as a software-defined network controller.
  • A measurement function that combines the ingress and egress measurements to assess the present level of congestion, for example by computing the loss rate for each interval from the difference between the two counter values. The method does not need high accuracy for the interval, since isolated and infrequent loss events are to be disregarded.
  • A trigger function that decides whether the measurements indicate persistent excessive congestion, by defining an appropriate threshold. It preferably considers a rate or ratio rather than an absolute value, for example more than 10% loss. The circuit breaker is triggered when the threshold is exceeded in multiple measurement intervals, for example three successive measurements, so that single or spurious events do not cause a reaction.
  • A reaction applied at the ingress when the circuit breaker triggers, which automatically removes the traffic causing the persistent excessive congestion.
  • A feedback control mechanism that triggers when either the ingress or egress measurements are not available, since that can also mean loss of control packets, which is itself a symptom of heavy congestion or an inability to control the load.
sections.plainLanguage: A circuit breaker needs to know how much traffic was sent and how much arrived, compare the two, and act at the sending end if the difference stays large. The two ends can be the endpoints of a flow or the two ends of a tunnel, and the measurements can travel in band with the traffic or out of band.

sections.title: Requirements for a Circuit Breaker
sections.content:
The document sets out seventeen requirements. The ones that shape the design most are these.

There must be a communication path for control messages to carry the measurement data from the two meters to the measurement function. A circuit breaker is REQUIRED to define a measurement period over which it measures the level of congestion or loss. The method does not have to detect individual packet loss, but it must have a way of knowing that packets were lost or marked. An egress meter may count congestion-experienced marks as part of the measurement, but in that case loss must also be measured to give a complete view.

The measurement period MUST be longer than the time current congestion control algorithms need to reduce their rate after detecting congestion, because end-to-end congestion control needs at least one round-trip time to notice and adjust, and congestion bottlenecks can share traffic with a wide range of round-trip times. A circuit breaker may combine successive meter samples to get an average over a long enough interval, in which case the combination has to divide the summed counts by the total time or volume over which they were measured.

A circuit breaker must not trigger under light or intermittent congestion. It is REQUIRED to define a threshold that decides whether the measured congestion is excessive, and a triggering interval over which the trigger uses the collected measurements. It must be robust to multiple congestion events, which usually means defining a number of measured persistent congestion events per triggering period, for example triggering when persistent excessive congestion is detected in three of the measurements within the triggering interval.

The normal reaction to a trigger SHOULD disable all the traffic that contributed to the congestion. The reaction MUST be much more severe than that of a congestion control algorithm, because the circuit breaker reacts to more persistent congestion over a longer timescale. A reaction that reduces traffic SHOULD reduce it by at least an order of magnitude, and terminating flows is often more desirable to users than randomly dropping packets. A circuit breaker that reduces the rate of a flow must keep monitoring and must react further if it is triggered again.

The reaction MUST continue for at least the triggering interval, and operator intervention will usually be needed to restore a flow. An automated reset, if there is one, must not be immediate, must not interact badly with other mechanisms, and SHOULD NOT reset when there is evidence of continued congestion.

A trigger should be regarded as an abnormal network event and SHOULD be logged, along with the measurements that led to it. The control communication may be in band or out of band, and in band is RECOMMENDED where both designs are possible, because it gives the traffic and the control messages a shared fate. The preferred design is one that triggers when it fails to receive measurement reports indicating an absence of congestion, rather than relying on a "congested" signal being delivered back, since that signal could itself be lost under congestion. An in-band method SHOULD treat loss of control messages as an indication of potential congestion, and repeated loss ought to cause the trigger. An out-of-band method SHOULD NOT trigger a reaction when control messages are lost, to avoid amplifying a failure when the measurement and data paths fail independently.

The control communication must be designed to be robust to packet loss, since a control message can be lost when the path fails and loss is likely during congestion. This does not imply a need for reliable delivery, since that can add delay in responding to congestion; duplicating control messages and treating a lack of control traffic as an indication of congestion are both appropriate. Control traffic over a shared path should be prioritised to reduce the chance of loss. The authenticity of the source and the integrity of the control messages must be protected from off-path attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules that matter most: wait much longer than a congestion control algorithm would, use a threshold and a triggering interval so one bad moment is not enough, and cut the traffic hard, by at least a factor of ten, and keep it cut until an operator intervenes.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Circuit Breaker
sections.content:
The document distinguishes three forms, mainly by the timescale over which they trigger and by the protection they offer.

A Fast-Trip circuit breaker is the most responsive form, with a response time only slightly larger than that of the traffic it controls. It suits traffic with well-understood characteristics and may use trigger functions tailored to that traffic. It is not suited to arbitrary network traffic and could be unsuitable for traffic aggregates, since it might trigger prematurely when the combined traffic from several congestion-controlled flows causes a short-term overload. The mechanisms can be implemented in RTP-aware network devices, and are also suitable for implementation in endpoints as part of the transport system, where they can complement end-to-end congestion control.

A set of Fast-Trip methods has been specified for use with an RTP flow using the RTP/AVP profile in RFC 8083. In the absence of severe congestion, all RTP applications running on best-effort IP networks are expected to run without triggering these circuit breakers, so an RTP Fast-Trip circuit breaker is a fail-safe that terminates the RTP traffic when it triggers. The sending endpoint monitors the reception report blocks in RTCP sender and receiver reports, which convey reception quality feedback, to measure congestion loss, possibly together with ECN. It triggers when there is a reported lack of progress, when no receiver reports arrive, when the long-term RTP throughput over many round-trip times exceeds a hard upper limit set by a method resembling TCP-Friendly Rate Control, or when the quality of the transported media falls below a required minimum.

A Slow-Trip circuit breaker is much slower to respond than a Fast-Trip one, and this is expected to be the more common form. One example of where it is needed is where flows or traffic aggregates use a tunnel and the flows inside it do not all support TCP-style congestion control. A use case is tunnels deployed in the general Internet rather than inside one operator's or enterprise's network, especially where the tunnel may cross a customer access router.

A Managed circuit breaker is implemented in the signalling protocol or management plane that relates to the traffic aggregate being controlled, and is typically applicable within a controlled environment. A circuit breaker needs more than the ability to see that a path is forwarding data or to measure its rate, which are normal operational functions: it needs a metric for congestion on the path and a trigger when a threshold is crossed.

Two managed examples are given. Section 8 of RFC 4553 describes a managed circuit breaker for isochronous flows over SAToP pseudowires. If the pseudowire traffic is multiplexed with other traffic over the general Internet it can experience congestion, and the recommended measurement period is 1 second, with the trigger operating when there are more than three measured Severely Errored Seconds within a period. The pseudowire then shuts down in both directions for some period. The reasoning is that a high loss ratio usually indicates something is broken and ought to have already resulted in operator intervention. An operator-based response gives the chance to restore service quality by shedding other loads or assigning more capacity, which can require the trigger to send a control message to a network operations centre rather than to the tunnel ingress itself. The second example concerns inelastic pseudowires such as fixed-bandwidth TDM, which do not adjust their rate when congestion appears and can therefore harm congestion-responsive traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Three time scales are described. A fast trip reacts almost as quickly as the traffic it guards and suits well-understood media streams. A slow trip reacts over longer periods and suits tunnels carrying mixed traffic. A managed breaker lives in the network's own signalling and is aimed at operators who can then fix the underlying problem.

sections.title: When a Circuit Breaker Is Not Needed
sections.content:
A circuit breaker is not required for a single congestion-controlled flow using TCP, SCTP or TFRC, because the congestion control methods there are already designed to prevent persistent excessive congestion.

For a tunnel deployed in a private network with pre-provisioned capacity, compliant traffic that does not exceed the provisioned capacity ought not to result in persistent congestion, so a circuit breaker would only be triggered by non-compliant traffic. Implementing one will not reduce the performance of the flows, but if persistent excessive congestion does occur it protects the traffic sharing that capacity, and it also protects the network from a failure in which circuit-breaker traffic is re-routed onto a path that was not pre-provisioned.

For a tunnel thought to carry only an aggregate of TCP traffic, TCP and SCTP traffic in a tunnel is expected to reduce its rate when congestion is detected, and other transports using UDP can employ sufficient mechanisms. Even so, the aggregate of many flows does not necessarily avoid persistent congestion: most congestion control mechanisms need long-lived flows to react, so an aggregate of many short flows could result in many flows ending before they experience congestion. It is also often impossible for a tunnel provider to know that the tunnel holds only congestion-controlled traffic, since inspecting packet headers may not be possible, and some applications may not implement adequate mechanisms. The important point is that if the aggregate does not result in persistent excessive congestion, the circuit breaker will not trigger, so implementing one ought not to reduce the performance of the tunnel.

A one-way forwarding path may have no communication path for control messages, and so cannot be controlled by a circuit breaker. A one-way service could use a path with dedicated pre-provisioned capacity not shared with other elastic flows, or a path shared with other flows, where ingress policing can manage the traffic envelope. Supporting this kind of traffic in the general Internet requires operator monitoring to detect and respond to persistent excessive congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: A circuit breaker is not needed for ordinary TCP traffic, and on a private network with reserved capacity it would never fire in normal operation. Adding one there costs nothing in performance and still covers the case where something goes wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All circuit breaker mechanisms rely on coordination between the ingress and egress meters and on communication with the trigger function, usually by passing network-control information across the network. The choice of measurement period matters for timely operation: if the receiver's interval is overly long, the responsiveness of the circuit breaker falls, and if it is too short the circuit breaker could trigger prematurely, leaving no time for other mechanisms to act and causing unnecessary disruption to the service.

A circuit breaker could be exploited by an attacker to mount a denial-of-service attack against the traffic it controls, so mechanisms need to prevent attacks on the network-control information that would result in one. The authenticity of the source and the integrity of the control messages must be protected from off-path attacks. Without that protection, it would be trivial for an attacker to inject fake or modified control and measurement messages, for example reporting a high packet loss rate, causing the circuit breaker to trigger and so disrupting a flow.

Simple protection comes from a randomised source port or an equivalent field in the packet header, such as the RTP SSRC value and the RTP sequence number, that an off-path attacker is not expected to know. Stronger protection comes from a secure authentication protocol. An attacker on the control path can attack messages that are neither encrypted nor authenticated, so using a cryptographic authentication mechanism for all control and measurement messages is RECOMMENDED. There is a trade-off between the cost of adding cryptographic protection and the value of protecting the control communication, and in some deployments that value leads to a requirement to authenticate all control messages.

Transmitting network-control messages consumes network capacity and could itself add to congestion, so it is RECOMMENDED that control traffic over a shared path be prioritised to reduce the probability of loss. The circuit breaker must be designed to be robust to packet loss, since loss of control messages can be a side effect of a congested network as well as having other causes. Each design must evaluate whether its particular mechanism brings new security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can forge the measurement messages could make the circuit breaker cut off traffic that was working fine, which is a denial-of-service attack. The control messages therefore need to be authenticated and protected from modification.

viz.caption: THE RULES THAT SHAPE A CIRCUIT BREAKER (RFC 8084, SECTION 4)

items.title: A long measurement period
items.text: It must be longer than the time congestion control needs to reduce its rate, so ordinary congestion does not trigger it.

items.title: A threshold and an interval
items.text: The trigger defines how bad the congestion must be and how long it must persist, for example three successive measurements.

items.title: A severe reaction
items.text: A reduction should cut the traffic by at least an order of magnitude, and terminating flows is often better than dropping packets.

items.title: It stays switched off
items.text: The reaction continues for at least the triggering interval, and an operator is usually needed to restore the flow.

items.title: In-band control preferred
items.text: Where both designs are possible, in-band control is recommended, so the control messages share the fate of the traffic.

items.title: Authenticated control messages
items.text: The source and integrity of the measurement and trigger messages must be protected from off-path attacks.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF CIRCUIT BREAKER (RFC 8084, SECTIONS 1.1 AND 5)

cells: Only slightly slower than the traffic it controls
Protecting a single flow or a related group of flows with well-understood characteristics
Much slower than a fast trip
Protecting traffic from congestion caused by traffic aggregates, such as a tunnel
Set by the signalling or management plane
Deployments inside a controlled environment, where an operator can act on the result

viz.caption: WHERE A CIRCUIT BREAKER IS NOT NEEDED (RFC 8084, SECTION 6)

items.title: A single congestion-controlled flow
items.text: TCP, SCTP and TFRC already prevent persistent excessive congestion.

items.title: A tunnel over pre-provisioned capacity
items.text: Compliant traffic should not congest the path, so the breaker would only fire on non-compliant traffic.

items.title: A tunnel carrying congestion-controlled traffic
items.text: If the aggregate does not congest the path, the breaker never triggers, so it costs nothing in performance.

items.title: Unidirectional traffic with no control path
items.text: Without a path for control messages the traffic cannot be controlled by a breaker at all.
